cloze.en: I live in Berlin now.

words.notes: Nominative (subject) form of the 1st person singular. Unlike English 'I', it is only capitalised at the start of a sentence.
words.mnemonic: ich → I; the accusative 'mich' and dative 'mir' both start with m- like 'me'.

example_sentences.de: Du sprichst schon sehr gut Deutsch.
example_sentences.en: You already speak German very well.

cloze.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

words.notes: Nominative of the 2nd person singular, informal. Accusative 'dich', dative 'dir'. With strangers and officials use 'Sie'.
words.germany_context: Germans use 'du' with friends, family, children and in most tech companies and startups, but stay with 'Sie' in shops, at the doctor and at the Bürgeramt. Let the older or more senior person offer the 'du' first.

example_sentences.de: Er heißt Thomas und ist mein Kollege.
example_sentences.en: His name is Thomas and he is my colleague.

example_sentences.de: Er arbeitet bei einer Firma in München.
example_sentences.en: He works at a company in Munich.

cloze.de: Wo ist Jan? ___ ist noch im Büro.
cloze.en: Where is Jan? He is still at the office.

words.notes: Nominative 3rd person masculine. It also replaces any masculine noun, not only people: 'Der Tisch? Er ist neu.'

cloze.de: Meine Frau? ___ arbeitet heute zu Hause.
cloze.en: My wife? She is working from home today.

words.notes: Nominative 3rd person feminine, written with a small s. Capital 'Sie' is the formal 'you'. It also replaces feminine nouns: 'Die Wohnung? Sie ist klein.'

cloze.en: How are you?

words.notes: Nominative and accusative of the 3rd person neuter — both forms are 'es'. It is also the dummy subject in weather and time phrases: 'Es regnet', 'Es ist acht Uhr'.

example_sentences.de: Wir wohnen seit einem Jahr in Köln.
example_sentences.en: We have been living in Cologne for a year.
We are going out to eat tonight.

cloze.de: ___ haben morgen einen Termin beim Amt.
cloze.en: We have an appointment at the public office tomorrow.

words.notes: Nominative 1st person plural. Its accusative and dative are both 'uns'.

cloze.en: Are you (all) coming along to the cinema?

words.notes: Nominative 2nd person plural, informal — 'you all'. Don't confuse it with possessive 'ihr' (her/their) or dative 'ihr' (to her); the verb ending -t marks this one: ihr kommt, ihr habt.

example_sentences.de: Meine Eltern? Sie besuchen mich im Sommer.
example_sentences.en: My parents? They are visiting me in the summer.

example_sentences.de: Ich kenne sie aus dem Deutschkurs.
example_sentences.en: I know them from the German course.

cloze.de: Wo sind die Kinder? ___ spielen im Hof.
cloze.en: Where are the children? They are playing in the courtyard.

words.notes: Nominative and accusative 3rd person plural — both are 'sie'. Identical in shape to 'sie' (she) and formal 'Sie'; the verb form and the context tell them apart. Dative is 'ihnen'.

cloze.en: Do you speak English?

words.notes: The polite 'you', always capitalised, used for one person or many. It takes the same verb form as 'sie' (they): Sie kommen, Sie haben.
words.germany_context: Default to 'Sie' with anyone you don't know: at the Bürgeramt, the doctor, the bank, your Vermieter and older neighbours. Using 'du' too early sounds rude; using 'Sie' too long only sounds polite.

example_sentences.en: He has known me for a long time.

cloze.en: The boss asked me yesterday.

words.notes: Accusative of 'ich' — the direct object. It is also the reflexive form: 'Ich wasche mich', 'Ich freue mich'.

cloze.en: Give me the key, please.

words.notes: Dative of 'ich' — the indirect object. Obligatory after helfen, danken, gehören, gefallen and after dative prepositions (mit, bei, von, zu, nach, aus, seit).
words.mnemonic: mir has an R like 'to me' — the R-form is the dative, the CH-form (mich) is the accusative.

example_sentences.de: Ich sehe dich morgen im Büro.
example_sentences.en: I'll see you tomorrow at the office.

cloze.en: Who took you to the station?

words.notes: Accusative of 'du'. Also the reflexive form: 'Setz dich!', 'Beeil dich!'

example_sentences.de: Ich schicke dir die Adresse per WhatsApp.
example_sentences.en: I'll send you the address on WhatsApp.

cloze.en: I'll buy you a coffee.

words.notes: Dative of 'du'. 'Wie geht es dir?' is the informal version of 'Wie geht es Ihnen?'

example_sentences.de: Ich kenne ihn von der Arbeit.

cloze.de: Den Vertrag? Ich habe ___ schon unterschrieben.
cloze.en: The contract? I have already signed it.

words.notes: Accusative of 'er'. It replaces masculine things as well as people: 'Der Kaffee? Ich trinke ihn schwarz.'

example_sentences.de: Ich habe ihm eine E-Mail geschrieben.
Hilf ihm bitte mit dem Formular!
example_sentences.en: Please help him with the form!

cloze.en: We'll give him the key tomorrow.

words.notes: Dative of 'er' and of 'es'. Learn the pair together: ihn = accusative, ihm = dative (m for 'mit dem' — dative).

example_sentences.de: Ich habe ihr beim Umzug geholfen.
example_sentences.en: I helped her with the move.

example_sentences.de: Gib ihr bitte das Buch zurück.
example_sentences.en: Please give the book back to her.

cloze.en: We are giving her flowers for her birthday.

words.notes: Dative of 'sie' (she). The accusative of 'sie' stays 'sie', so only the dative changes shape — that is why 'Ich sehe sie' but 'Ich helfe ihr'.

example_sentences.de: Kannst du uns vom Bahnhof abholen?
example_sentences.en: Can you pick us up from the station?

cloze.de: Ruf ___ bitte an, wenn du da bist.
cloze.en: Please call us when you are here.

words.notes: Accusative and dative of 'wir' — one form covers both cases. Also reflexive: 'Wir treffen uns um acht.'

example_sentences.en: I'll visit you (all) at the weekend.

cloze.de: Ich schicke ___ die Fotos heute Abend.
cloze.en: I'll send you (all) the photos tonight.

words.notes: Accusative and dative of 'ihr' (you plural) — one form for both. Also reflexive: 'Setzt euch!'

example_sentences.de: Ich habe ihnen die Wohnung gezeigt.

example_sentences.en: Does the car belong to them?

cloze.en: We wrote to them yesterday.

words.notes: Dative of 'sie' (they), written with a small i. The accusative of 'they' is simply 'sie'. Capitalised 'Ihnen' is the formal 'to you'.

cloze.de: Ich schicke ___ die Unterlagen per E-Mail.
cloze.en: I'll send you the documents by email.

words.notes: Dative of the formal 'Sie', always capitalised. 'Kann ich Ihnen helfen?' is the standard opener from shop and office staff.
words.germany_context: 'Kann ich Ihnen helfen?' is how counter and shop staff open, and 'Haben Sie einen Termin?' is usually the next question. Answer 'Ich habe einen Termin um 10 Uhr' or 'Nein, leider nicht'.

cloze.en: My apartment is on the third floor.

words.notes: Possessive article. It takes exactly the endings of 'ein': mein Mann, meine Frau, mein Kind, meine Eltern, meinen Bruder (accusative).
words.germany_context: Your surname must be on the Klingelschild (doorbell sign) and the Briefkasten. German post and parcel services do not deliver to an unnamed letterbox, and Amt letters simply go back to the sender.

cloze.en: Where are your keys?

words.notes: Possessive article belonging to 'du'. Same endings as 'ein': dein Vater, deine Mutter, dein Kind, deinen Ausweis (accusative).

cloze.en: He is looking for his phone.

words.notes: Possessive article for 'er' and 'es'. It looks identical to the verb 'sein' (to be) — if it stands directly in front of a noun, it means 'his/its'.

cloze.en: Anna forgot her phone.

words.notes: Possessive article meaning 'her' (for singular 'sie') and 'their' (for plural 'sie'). Written with a capital I it becomes the formal 'your'.

example_sentences.de: Unser Sohn geht in die Kita.

cloze.en: Our neighbours are very nice.

words.notes: Possessive article for 'wir'. The endings are added to the full stem: unser Haus, unsere Wohnung, unseren Vermieter, unseren Kindern.

cloze.en: What is your new address?

words.notes: Possessive article for 'ihr' (you plural). The -e- of the stem drops as soon as an ending is added: euer Auto, but eure Wohnung, euren Freunden.

cloze.en: Please sign your application here.

words.notes: Possessive article for the formal 'Sie', always with a capital I. Standard in official letters: 'Ihr Antrag', 'Ihre Anmeldung', 'Ihr Schreiben vom 3. August'.
words.germany_context: German authorities still decide most things on paper. Letters open with 'Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren' and refer to 'Ihr Antrag' or 'Ihr Schreiben' — check your Briefkasten regularly, deadlines in those letters are binding.

cloze.en: This bus goes to the main station.

words.notes: Masculine nominative of the demonstrative 'this'. It takes der-endings: dieser Mann (nom), diesen Mann (akk), diesem Mann (dat).
words.mnemonic: dies- + der-endings: dieser / diese / dieses, like der / die / das.
words.germany_context: Termine run daily life here — Bürgeramt, doctors, even phone shops. Slots open online weeks ahead, so book the Termin first and worry about 'Dieser Termin passt mir' second.

cloze.de: ___ Woche habe ich viel zu tun.
cloze.en: This week I have a lot to do.

words.notes: Covers two slots: feminine singular (diese Frau) and all plurals (diese Leute), in nominative and accusative. 'diese Woche' = this week, 'diesen Monat' = this month.

example_sentences.en: You have to fill in this form.

example_sentences.de: Dieses Jahr bleiben wir in Deutschland.
example_sentences.en: This year we are staying in Germany.

cloze.en: This house belongs to my landlord.

words.notes: Neuter nominative and accusative. In relaxed speech people often point instead and say 'das da' — but 'dieses Jahr' and 'dieses Wochenende' are used constantly.

example_sentences.de: Dieses Buch ist neu, jenes ist alt.
example_sentences.en: This book is new, that one is old.

example_sentences.de: In jener Zeit gab es noch keine Handys.
example_sentences.en: In those days there were no mobile phones yet.

cloze.de: Nicht dieser Zug fährt nach Hamburg, sondern ___ dort.
cloze.en: It's not this train that goes to Hamburg, but that one over there.

words.notes: The formal, rather literary 'that'. Almost nobody says it in spoken German — people say 'der da' / 'das da' instead. Worth recognising in written texts, not worth producing.

cloze.en: That was a very good film.

words.notes: Demonstrative pronoun 'this/that'. It stays 'das' whatever follows: 'Das ist mein Mann', 'Das ist meine Frau', 'Das sind meine Kinder'. Don't confuse it with the article 'das' or the conjunction 'dass'.

example_sentences.de: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
example_sentences.en: How do you say that in German?

cloze.de: Am Sonntag kann ___ hier nicht einkaufen.
cloze.en: On Sunday you can't go shopping here.

words.notes: Impersonal subject pronoun — nominative only, always with the er/sie/es verb form. It is not 'der Mann' (the man): one n, no capital.
words.mnemonic: one n = 'one'; two n's = ein Mann.
words.germany_context: 'man' is the voice of every rule sign in Germany. Ruhezeit is real: between 22:00 and 06:00, plus all day Sunday, man darf keinen Lärm machen — no drilling, no loud music, in many buildings no washing machine.

cloze.de: Kennst du hier ___, der Türkisch spricht?
cloze.en: Do you know anyone here who speaks Turkish?

words.notes: Indefinite pronoun, singular only. Accusative 'jemanden', dative 'jemandem' — in casual speech the endings are often dropped.

example_sentences.en: I don't know anyone here yet.

cloze.en: Nobody opened the door.

words.notes: The negative counterpart of 'jemand'. Accusative 'niemanden', dative 'niemandem'. Never combine it with a second negation.
words.germany_context: If niemand is home, DHL or Hermes usually leaves your parcel with a neighbour or at a Paketshop and drops a Benachrichtigungskarte in the Briefkasten. Take that card plus your Ausweis to collect it.

example_sentences.en: I would like something to drink.

cloze.en: I have forgotten something important.

words.notes: Means 'something' as a pronoun and 'a bit' in front of adjectives ('etwas teuer' = a bit expensive). In speech it is usually shortened to 'was': 'Willst du was essen?'

example_sentences.en: There is nothing left in the fridge.

cloze.en: He didn't understand anything.

words.notes: 'nothing' — one negation is enough: 'Ich habe nichts gesagt', never 'nichts nicht'. Don't mix it up with 'nicht' (= not), which negates verbs and adjectives.

example_sentences.de: Alle Kollegen sind heute im Büro.
example_sentences.en: All the colleagues are in the office today.

cloze.de: ___ Flaschen mit Pfand kann man zurückbringen.
cloze.en: You can return all bottles that have a deposit.

words.notes: The plural form: 'all the ...' with things, 'everybody' with people. For an uncountable whole use 'alles' (everything).
words.germany_context: Pfand: cans and plastic bottles carry 0,25 €, most glass bottles 0,08-0,15 €. Feed them into the Automat at the supermarket entrance and hand the printed Bon in at the till — it comes off your shopping bill.

cloze.en: Did you understand everything?

words.notes: Neuter singular 'everything'. 'Alles klar!' and 'Alles gut!' are the everyday way of saying 'got it' / 'no problem'.
words.germany_context: When a flat ad says a price, ask what is included: Kaltmiete is the bare rent, Nebenkosten (water, rubbish, heating, Hausmeister) come on top and together they make the Warmmiete. Strom and internet are almost always separate contracts you sign yourself.

example_sentences.de: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem Rad zur Arbeit.
example_sentences.en: I cycle to work every day.

cloze.en: The shops are closed every Sunday.

words.notes: Singular only, with der-endings: jeder Mann, jede Frau, jedes Kind. Time expressions take the accusative: jeden Tag, jede Woche, jedes Jahr.
words.germany_context: Nearly every shop and supermarket is shut on Sundays and public holidays. The exceptions: bakeries for a few morning hours, petrol stations, and shops inside big train stations and airports. Do the week's shopping by Saturday evening.

example_sentences.de: Ich habe noch einige Fragen zum Vertrag.
example_sentences.en: I still have a few questions about the contract.

cloze.en: We have been waiting for several minutes already.

words.notes: Plural 'some / several' — more than 'ein paar', fewer than 'viele'. Dative plural takes -n: 'seit einigen Tagen', 'mit einigen Freunden'.

example_sentences.de: Viele Leute fahren hier mit dem Fahrrad.
Ich habe viele Fragen zum Mietvertrag.
example_sentences.en: I have a lot of questions about the rental contract.

cloze.en: There are many cafes in Berlin.

words.notes: Plural of 'viel'. Countable plural → viele (viele Freunde); uncountable singular stays viel (viel Zeit, viel Geld).

example_sentences.de: Nur wenige Geschäfte haben sonntags offen.
example_sentences.en: Only a few shops are open on Sundays.

example_sentences.de: Wenige Leute waren um sechs Uhr im Bus.
example_sentences.en: Few people were on the bus at six o'clock.

cloze.en: So far I only know a few neighbours here.

words.notes: Plural 'few' (= not many). The uncountable singular is 'wenig' (wenig Zeit), and 'ein wenig' means 'a little bit'.

cloze.en: Both children go to the same school.

words.notes: Plural only, and only for exactly two. After a definite article it takes -n: 'die beiden Brüder', 'meine beiden Koffer'.

cloze.en: I'd rather take a different room.

words.notes: Behaves like an adjective and takes adjective endings: ein anderer Termin, eine andere Wohnung, ein anderes Zimmer, die anderen Leute.

cloze.de: Tut mir leid, wir nehmen ___ Karten.
cloze.en: Sorry, we don't take cards.

words.notes: The negative article. Use it, not 'nicht', in front of a noun that would otherwise have 'ein' or no article: 'Ich habe kein Auto' (never 'nicht ein Auto'). Endings like 'ein', plus a plural: keine Kinder.
words.germany_context: 'Nur Bargeld' and 'Wir nehmen keine Karten' are still normal in Bäckereien, Kiosks, Imbisse, small Cafés and even some doctors' practices. Carry 20-50 € cash at all times.

example_sentences.en: Some people use 'du' with each other right away.

example_sentences.de: Manche Geschäfte haben samstags nur bis 16 Uhr offen.
example_sentences.en: Some shops are only open until 4 p.m. on Saturdays.

cloze.en: Some colleagues work only from home.

words.notes: Plural 'some, but not all'. More selective than 'einige': it sets one group against another. Takes der-endings: manche Leute, manchen Kollegen (dative).

example_sentences.de: Das ist der Kollege, der mir geholfen hat.
example_sentences.en: That is the colleague who helped me.

example_sentences.de: Der Mann, der unten wohnt, ist der Hausmeister.
example_sentences.en: The man who lives downstairs is the caretaker.

cloze.de: Ich habe einen Freund, ___ in München wohnt.
cloze.en: I have a friend who lives in Munich.

words.notes: Relative pronoun for a masculine subject — the same shape as the article 'der'. A comma always comes before it and the verb moves to the end of the clause. Feminine: die, neuter: das, plural: die.
words.germany_context: Every apartment building has a Hausmeister: he handles the heating, the Treppenhaus cleaning rota, the bins and small repairs. For a broken lock or a dripping tap you call him first, the Vermieter second.

example_sentences.de: Die Kinder freuen sich auf den Sommer.
example_sentences.en: The children are looking forward to the summer.

cloze.de: Man muss ___ innerhalb von 14 Tagen anmelden.
cloze.en: You have to register within 14 days.

words.notes: Reflexive pronoun for er/sie/es, plural sie and formal Sie — accusative and dative are both 'sich'. For ich/du/wir/ihr you use mich/dich/uns/euch instead. It is the form you see in dictionaries: 'sich freuen', 'sich anmelden'.
words.germany_context: Anmeldung: after moving in you must register your address at the Bürgeramt, in most cities within 14 days. Bring the Wohnungsgeberbestätigung from your landlord — without the Anmeldebestätigung there is no bank account, no Steuer-ID and no phone contract.

cloze.en: I assembled the furniture myself.

words.notes: Emphatic 'myself/yourself/himself' — it never changes form. In front of a noun it can also mean 'even': 'Selbst am Sonntag arbeitet er.' The colloquial variant is 'selber'.
words.germany_context: 'Selbstauskunft' is the SCHUFA credit report landlords ask for with practically every rental application, together with your last three Gehaltsabrechnungen and a copy of your Ausweis. Order it early — the free version can take weeks by post.

example_sentences.en: What do you do for a living?

cloze.en: What would you like to drink?

words.notes: Question word 'what' — nominative and accusative are both 'was'. In casual speech it also stands in for 'etwas': 'Ich hab was vergessen.'
words.germany_context: 'Was macht das?' is how you ask for the total. Trinkgeld is 5-10%, rounded up, and you say the full amount out loud as you hand the money over ('Machen Sie 25') — you don't leave coins on the table.

example_sentences.en: Who did you say that to?

cloze.en: Who did you speak to?

words.notes: Dative of 'wer'. Required after gehören, helfen, danken and after every dative preposition: 'Mit wem?', 'Von wem?', 'Bei wem?'.
words.germany_context: Kaution: the rental deposit is up to three months' Kaltmiete. The landlord must hold it in a separate account and pay it back with interest — but usually only three to six months after you move out, once the Nebenkostenabrechnung is settled.
